write.desc: This topic sets up the least upper bound: what upper and lower bounds, supremum and infimum are, the completeness axiom that guarantees they exist, the epsilon characterisation, and the practice of proving sup and inf statements directly from the definition. These are one connected toolkit, and every later existence proof in the course rests on it.

points.name: Upper and lower bounds, maximum and minimum
points.what: The learner can say what it means for a set of reals to be bounded above, bounded below or bounded, and what its maximum and minimum are. They can show from the definitions that a given set is or is not bounded, including writing out the negation 'for every M there is s in S with s > M'.
outside: order axioms of the real numbers (the order relation and its rules)

points.name: Supremum and infimum: the definitions
points.what: The learner knows the supremum as the least upper bound (an upper bound u with u <= v for every upper bound v) and the infimum as the greatest lower bound. They can prove that a set has at most one supremum, and that a set has a maximum exactly when its supremum exists and belongs to it.

points.name: Sup and inf of simple sets: attained or not
points.what: The learner can find and justify the sup and inf of sets such as finite sets, [0,1], [0,1), (0,1] and {1 - 1/n : n in N}. They can tell when the supremum is attained (a maximum) and when it is not, for example proving sup [0,1) = 1 by showing that any u < 1 is beaten by the midpoint (u + 1)/2.

points.name: Proving a supremum in two steps: upper bound, then least
points.what: The learner has the habit of proving u = sup S as two separate claims: first that every s in S satisfies s <= u, then that no smaller number is an upper bound (any upper bound v has u <= v, or any v < u is exceeded by some s in S). They use scratch work to find the element or the bound before writing the proof cleanly.

points.name: The completeness axiom
points.what: The learner can state the least upper bound axiom: every non-empty set of reals that is bounded above has a supremum in R. They understand that it is the axiom that makes R a complete ordered field and that the other ordered field axioms, which Q also satisfies, cannot give it.
outside: the real numbers as an ordered field (field and order axioms)

points.name: Infimum version of completeness: inf S = -sup(-S)
points.what: The learner can prove that every non-empty set bounded below has an infimum, by showing inf S = -sup(-S) where -S = {-s : s in S}. They can move freely between statements about sup and statements about inf.
outside: multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses it

points.name: The epsilon characterisation of sup and inf
points.what: The learner can prove and use the criterion: an upper bound u of S is sup S exactly when for every epsilon > 0 there is s in S with s > u - epsilon; and a lower bound l is inf S exactly when for every epsilon > 0 there is s in S with s < l + epsilon. They use it both to prove a number is the supremum and to pick elements of S close to the supremum.

points.name: Comparing sups of sets: subsets and separated sets
points.what: The learner can prove that if A is a non-empty subset of B and B is bounded then inf B <= inf A <= sup A <= sup B, and that if a <= b for every a in A and b in B then sup A <= inf B. They see these as the basic comparison tools for later arguments.

points.name: Supremum of a sum of sets: sup(A + B) = sup A + sup B
points.what: The learner can prove that for non-empty sets bounded above, A + B = {a + b} has supremum sup A + sup B, giving the upper bound step directly and the 'least' step either with the epsilon characterisation (using epsilon/2 for each set) or by fixing one element at a time. They can state and prove the matching result for inf and for translates c + A.

points.name: Scaling a set: sup(cA) for c > 0 and c < 0
points.what: The learner can prove that sup(cA) = c sup A when c > 0, and that sup(cA) = c inf A when c < 0, so multiplying by a negative number swaps sup and inf. They can handle the analogous statements for inf and the case c = 0.
outside: multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses it

points.name: Sup and inf of function values
points.what: The learner can work with sup and inf of the set of values {f(x) : x in D} of a bounded function, prove facts such as sup (f + g) <= sup f + sup g and inf f + inf g <= inf (f + g), and give examples where the inequalities are strict. They can prove 'if f(x) <= g(x) for all x then sup f <= sup g' and similar statements later used for Darboux sums.
outside: functions, domain and the image of a set

points.name: The rationals are not complete: {x in Q : x^2 < 2}
points.what: The learner can explain why the set of rationals with x^2 < 2 is non-empty and bounded above in Q but has no least upper bound in Q, using that no rational squares to 2 and that rationals can be nudged closer to sqrt 2 from either side. They understand this as the example showing that completeness is a genuine extra property; the existence of sqrt 2 in R is proved in the next topic.

points.name: Where the reals come from: a mention of their construction
points.what: The learner knows that R can be built from Q, by Dedekind cuts or by equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences, so that the complete ordered field assumed in the course really exists, and that this construction is not needed to use completeness.

points.name: Extended reals and sup S = +infinity as notation
points.what: The learner can read and use the notation sup S = +infinity for a set unbounded above and inf S = -infinity for a set unbounded below, understanding that +infinity and -infinity are symbols in the extended reals and not real numbers to compute with.

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis (4th ed.)
where.detail: Section 2.3, The Completeness Property of R; Section 2.4, Applications of the Supremum Property

where.title: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd ed.)
where.detail: Chapter 1, ordered sets and the least-upper-bound property; appendix to Chapter 1 for the Dedekind cut construction

where.title: Terence Tao, Analysis I
where.detail: Section 5.5, The least upper bound property
